newsitem.title: UK: SEGERS SHOULD BE CLEARED OF UK SOCCER CHARGES - LAWYER.
newsitem.headline: SEGERS SHOULD BE CLEARED OF UK SOCCER CHARGES - LAWYER.

text.p: Former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers should be found not guilty of match-fixing charges because there is no evidence at all against him, the soccer star's lawyer said on Tuesday.

"The prosecution cannot point to any match or any game which they say Segers threw. There is not one shred of positive evidence that Segers threw a match," Desmond Da Silva told a court in the south-western city of Winchester.
"Look at him -- is he the sort of inhabitant of the dark corners of a corrupted game?" he said in an impassioned final speech to the jury, pointing to the Dutch-born goalkeeper.
"I invite you, in this desperately serious case, to free him and his family from the agony which has been hanging over them for the last two years."

Segers and former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar are accused of taking money from ex-Wimbledon striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim to throw games for an Asian betting syndicate.
Lim admits he paid the two goalkeepers to forecast the results of matches but all four deny rigging games. The jury is expected to start considering its verdict next Monday.
Da Silva said Segers faced an uncertain future since match forecasting was against Football Association rules and he had not declared his earnings to the Inland Revenue tax service.
"If you find Segers not guilty, his problems will not be over. You may think there will be a lot in store from the Inland Revenue and the Football Association," he said.
The lawyer accused the prosecution of misleading the jury by focusing on 19 games Segers played in during the 1993/4 and 1994/5 seasons, most of which Wimbledon lost.
"What the schedule did not show was that some 24 matches in which he played were left out. Not one of them was lost. Nineteen were won and five were drawn," he said.
The 1993/4 season was the most successful in Wimbledon's history and the club finished sixth in the premier division.
"It doesn't take a genius to work out that Wimbledon did so brilliantly because Segers was doing his part in saving goals, not throwing them, and by winning matches, not losing them," said Da Silva.
The prosecution focused on 104,000 pounds (about $170,000) which Segers paid into a Swiss bank account over 13 months, suggesting the money was a reward for throwing games.
Da Silva told the court that part of the money had come from Lim for forecasting Dutch soccer matches and part was the proceeds of a tie-making company Segers had set up.

Segers, worried about being banned from soccer because of his involvement in match-forecasting, lied to police about the money and said it had come from the proceeds of car thefts carried out when a teenager in the Netherlands.
"If you forgive me for saying so, you can see how extremely stupid he was....the truth is, it was a stupid story stupidly told that fooled no one," Da Silva said.
